tagline.text: The Philippines' largest protected area, with primary forest and a remote coast around Palanan

location.label: Location
location.text: Eastern Isabela around Palanan, Divilacan and Maconacon (including parts of Ilagan, San Mariano, Tumauini and others)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: March–May dry period (best time to reach remote areas)

budget.label: Budget

children.text: Northern Sierra Madre Natural Park covers about 359,486 hectares, making it the largest protected area in the Philippines, and takes in the primary forests of the northern Sierra Madre and the Palanan coast. Access is difficult and needs small planes, boats or hiking, so it is an expedition-style destination.

Northern Sierra Madre Natural Park is the largest protected area in the Philippines, in the province of Isabela in eastern Luzon. According to Wikipedia, its total area is 359,486 hectares, of which 287,861 hectares are land and 71,652 hectares are coastal waters. It is centered on the municipalities of Palanan, Divilacan and Maconacon, and also includes parts of San Mariano, Dinapigue, San Pablo, Cabagan, Tumauini and Ilagan City. It faces the Cagayan Valley to the west and the Philippine Sea to the east, and is regarded as the richest area in the Philippines in genetic, species and habitat diversity.

The park was designated in two steps. On September 7, 1979, Letter of Instructions No. 917-A signed by President Marcos established the Palanan Wilderness Area within a 45 km radius of Palanan Point, and on March 10, 1997, President Ramos's Proclamation No. 978 made it a natural park. Republic Act No. 9125 (the Northern Sierra Madre Natural Park Act of 2001) set the framework for its management, which is overseen by a Protected Area Management Board headed by the DENR Regional Executive Director. In 2006 it was added to the Philippines' tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage. Wikipedia's article on Palanan says the wilderness area was proclaimed in 1978 under Marcos, so the years differ.

The natural environment has two main forest types. Below about 1,000 m are Luzon rain forests with tall dipterocarps such as Shorea and Hopea, and above that are montane rain forests dominated by oaks and laurels. The highest peak is Mount Cresta (1,672 m) on the western ridge, and the second highest is Mount Divilacan (1,311 m) on the eastern side. Fourteen major rivers drain the park: 11 flow into the Philippine Sea and 3 into the Ilagan River. The largest, the Palanan River, drains about 29% of the park. Rare and endangered species reported include the Philippine eagle, the giant golden-crowned flying fox, the Philippine eagle-owl, the Isabela oriole, green, loggerhead and hawksbill sea turtles, the Philippine crocodile and the dugong.

The human story is deep as well. Indigenous Dumagat and Agta communities live in the park, and Palanan is the historic place where Emilio Aguinaldo was captured by US forces on March 23, 1901, the last capital he had used (Wikipedia). The town of Palanan was founded on July 22, 1609 by Spanish forces who crossed by boat from Baler. The park is therefore both a protected forest and a site of Philippine independence history.

About 359,486 hectares of forest and sea form one continuous area. It is counted among the country's ten priority protected areas, and a distinguishing feature is that ecosystems run unbroken from the western mountains to the eastern coast.

In Barangay San Isidro, Palanan, there is a beach about 3 km long with coral, seagrass beds and a coastal forest. To reach it, take a tricycle to Culasi village and then a boat. Check details separately.
A clear body of water about 15–20 minutes by tricycle from Palanan town, named by one traveler as a favorite. Simple cottages let you leave your belongings and rest for an hour or two.

blocks.title: Aguinaldo Shrine and St. Mary Magdalene Church

children.text: In the center of Palanan town there is a memorial to the place of Aguinaldo's last stand, with St. Mary Magdalene Parish across from it. The church belfry reportedly has bells about 300 years old.

About 30 minutes on foot from Dicotcotan is a seaside community of the Agta people, and Diago Beach lies across from it. The sand is whiter and there are rock formations. Respect local culture when you visit.
The Palanan River, surrounded by forest, is described as good for swimming and rafting. Disadsad Falls is a 15–20 minute boat ride plus about 1 hour on foot.
At Digoyo Point you can see the wreck of MV Karagatan, a 1970s ship, on dives, and the surrounding coral gardens are good for snorkeling. Check safety conditions with local operators.
One traveler describes it as one of the cleanest rivers in the country. The current is moderate, so take care when swimming. Sumalag Falls has no pool to swim in.

items.title: Five days, four nights in Palanan
items.subtitle: Flying in for the coast and villages

children.text: Travel from Manila to Cauayan. Cebu Pacific reportedly flew Manila–Cauayan (as of 2019).
Fly from Cauayan to Palanan on a small plane; the flight takes about 30 minutes. Settle into your lodging and see the Aguinaldo Shrine and church in town.
Visit Blue Lagoon and walk to Dicotcotan Beach, the Dumagat village and Diago Beach.
Charter a boat to tour the coasts of Palanan, Divilacan and Maconacon. In Maconacon you can see the Blos River.
Fly back to Cauayan on a small plane and continue toward Manila.
One 2019 review's itinerary was five days, and a packaged joiner tour reportedly cost about ₱9,000 per person. Small planes and boats can be canceled by weather, so keep a spare day.

items.title: Overland and sea expedition
items.subtitle: Seven days or more across sea and mountains

children.text: Travel from Manila via Cabanatuan and Baler to Dilasag or Dingalan in Aurora.
Take a large outrigger boat (lancha) from Dilasag (or Dingalan or Baler) to Palanan, about 6–7 hours.
Walk around Palanan and tour the coast.
Fly back on a small plane, or, for experienced groups, attempt the 3–5 day river-trek crossing to San Mariano. Always take a local guide on this route.
The overland itinerary depends heavily on weather and boat operations. Leave plenty of spare time.

One travel information site gives annual rainfall of about 2,768 mm, with November the wettest. Modeled climate data for Palanan town gives average highs of

November–May is the dry period, and some say March–May is the most stable. June–October brings typhoons and the rainy season, when small planes and boats are easily canceled and rivers rise dangerously.

On Dicotcotan Beach in Palanan there is the Bilay Makadawi Beach Resort, described as having cottages and treehouses. It reportedly arranges itineraries, transfers and tours, and you need to ask for rates. Near Blue Lagoon there are simple cottages.

Meals often depend on your lodging's restaurant. In Maconacon, tricycles run from the port to town and you can rent a private jeep for sightseeing. Because the area is remote, bring plenty of food, water, cash and basic medicine. No confirmed information is available on phone signal and electricity, so bring a power bank.
First find a place (a resort or local tour operator) that can handle both bookings and transport. One traveler says a resort arranged boat transfers.
Small planes have strict baggage limits, so pack light and check with the operator beforehand.
Flights and boats can be canceled by weather, so leave spare days before your departure flight home.
Areas inside the park may require a permit, so check permit and guide rules with the DENR regional office or the local tourism office.
When visiting Dumagat and Agta villages, respect residents' privacy and ask permission before taking photos.
Bring plenty of cash. Cards and currency exchange may be hard to find locally.
Price information comes mostly from old reviews, so reconfirm rates just before departure.
Northern Sierra Madre is a remote area without roads. Small planes, boats and hiking are all heavily affected by weather, and medical and communication facilities are limited, so prepare thoroughly.
No official information on entrance and permit fees and guide rules could be found. Even the descriptions of the entrance permit on one site gave inconsistent amounts, so confirm locally.
Some sources point to continuing illegal logging inside the park, and news reports urge local communities to protect the forest. Carry your trash out and do not take part in harming nature.
River crossings on foot are dangerous because rivers rise quickly when it rains, so do not attempt them without an experienced guide.
Some reviews are old, so infrastructure such as the Ilagan–Divilacan road may have changed.
Do not approach or feed wildlife, including snakes. Seeing a Philippine eagle is reportedly very rare.
A protected area in Ilagan, Isabela, with caves and a tree-top adventure. It is easier to reach than Northern Sierra Madre Natural Park and suits beginners.
A large multipurpose dam in Ramon, Isabela. It is easy to reach and can be combined in the same regional itinerary.
A surfing town in Aurora and one of the starting points for reaching Palanan by boat or road.
A coastal town in Aurora from which boats toward Palanan reportedly depart.
